title: Preprocessor directives, macros and conditional compilation
learningObjectives: Explain that preprocessing handles directives before ordinary C translation and identify the role of #include, #define, #if, #ifdef and #endif.
Distinguish object-like macros from function-like macros and understand that substitution operates on preprocessing tokens.
Use include guards or an equivalent supported mechanism to prevent repeated header inclusion.
Parenthesize macro parameters and replacement expressions and avoid arguments with side effects when a macro may evaluate them more than once.
Use conditional compilation for deliberate configuration while keeping all supported configurations syntactically valid.
Prefer typed functions, enum constants or const objects when they provide safer semantics than a macro.

understand.concept: The preprocessor processes directives such as #include, #define, #if, #ifdef and #endif before the compiler analyzes the resulting translation unit. Object-like macros replace a name with tokens; function-like macros substitute arguments into a token sequence. Macros are not ordinary functions: they do not provide normal parameter type checking, and an argument may be evaluated more than once.
understand.whyItMatters: Macros support include guards, compile-time configuration and conditional code, but careless expansion can change operator precedence, duplicate side effects or create confusing diagnostics. Understanding the preprocessing stage helps explain why the compiler sees different source under different configurations.
understand.analogy: A macro is like a text-template substitution performed before the compiler reads the completed program.
understand.analogyLimit: The template analogy is limited: preprocessing works on tokens and has detailed rules for stringification, token pasting and rescanning; it is not a general text editor or a type-aware function call.

explain.narrative: An object-like macro such as #define LIMIT 100 replaces the macro name with its replacement tokens. A function-like macro such as #define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x)) substitutes tokens for its parameter. Parentheses protect grouping, but they do not prevent repeated evaluation: SQUARE(i++) is unsafe because the argument can be evaluated more than once. Prefer a function when ordinary evaluation and type checking are needed.\n\nA header guard uses #ifndef, #define and #endif to prevent the same header contents from being processed repeatedly in one translation unit. The guard macro should be unique to the header. Conditional compilation can select code using macros defined by the build, but every supported configuration must remain valid C. Use #if for numeric preprocessor expressions and #ifdef when testing whether a macro is defined. The preprocessor does not understand C variable values or runtime conditions.

examples.title: Guard a header and declare a shared interface
examples.explanation: The include guard prevents duplicate declarations if the header is included more than once in the same translation unit. This compact teaching example places the function definition in main.c; a multi-file project would put it in a separate source file.

examples.title: Use a macro without duplicating a side effect
examples.explanation: Both forms produce 25 for a side-effect-free argument. The function has an ordinary typed parameter and evaluates its argument once. Do not pass expressions such as number++ to a macro that substitutes its parameter multiple times.

practise.guidedTask: Expand SQUARE(a + b) by hand, then explain why SQUARE(i++) can modify i more than once. Inspect a header guard and identify which directives prevent repeated inclusion.
practise.independentTask: Create a header with a unique include guard, one declaration and a configuration macro. Build a small program in two configurations and explain what the preprocessor includes in each.
hints: The # in a directive must appear where the preprocessing grammar permits it.
Macro arguments are token sequences, not typed function parameters.
Parenthesize each parameter use and the complete replacement expression.
Avoid side effects in arguments to function-like macros.
Use unique include-guard names to avoid collisions.
A compile-time #if is not a runtime if statement.

options: Before ordinary C translation of the resulting translation unit
Only when a function is called
questions.answer: Before ordinary C translation of the resulting translation unit
questions.explanation: The preprocessor handles directives before the compiler analyzes the resulting C translation unit.

questions.prompt: What is a major risk of a macro such as SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))?
options: An argument with side effects may be evaluated more than once
It is executed only at link time
questions.answer: An argument with side effects may be evaluated more than once
questions.explanation: Token substitution can duplicate an argument expression, unlike a normal function parameter evaluation.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a header guard?
options: Prevent repeated processing of a header's contents in one translation unit
Make every function in the header static
questions.answer: Prevent repeated processing of a header's contents in one translation unit
questions.explanation: The preprocessor macro guard causes later inclusions to skip the guarded contents.

questions.prompt: Which construct tests whether a macro is defined?
questions.explanation: #ifdef checks whether a macro name has been defined.

questions.prompt: When is a function usually safer than a function-like macro?
options: When ordinary type checking and single evaluation of arguments are desired
questions.answer: When ordinary type checking and single evaluation of arguments are desired
questions.explanation: A function has typed parameters and each argument expression is evaluated as part of the call.
